# Weekly tales and side quests

> **Spoilers.** This page reveals the story as it unfolds through the year. Read the world and district pages first if you want to discover it in the game.

## Weekly tales

One short tale each week of the year, shown on the map.

### Week 1: The First Lamp

Dusk on Lamplighters' Quay. Forty-four iron posts stand along the water like a row of tall, patient herons, every one of them dark. Wren hands you a list of the things the fishermen are afraid of losing tonight. "Start with the first post," she says. "Hold every one of these as a picture, and see if the lamp takes." The mist is already coming up off the river.

### Week 2: Tansy's Advice

An old woman with a tea stall under the last lamp watches you work for a whole evening without a word. Then she presses a hot cup of rosemary tea into your hands. "You're holding them one at a time," she says. "Make them hold hands. The net remembers the boat, the boat remembers the gull. Nothing in this world is alone, love. Don't make your pictures lonely."

### Week 3: Lamps Going Out

You come down to the Quay one morning and find six of your lamps cold, their glass fogged silver on the inside. Mosk the ferryman shows you a footprint in the river mud: the long, soft print of a bare foot. "Hushed," he mutters. "They walk barefoot so the stones won't hear them." Tonight you will stay to watch.

### Week 4: Under the Last Lamp

Wren has borrowed a cudgel from the ferryman and is holding it like a soup ladle. "If anybody asks," she whispers, "I'm very dangerous." The mist thickens. Somewhere down the Quay, a lamp goes out with a small, sad sound, like someone blowing out a birthday candle. Then another. They are coming this way.

### Week 5: The Blank Gallery

A mile of honey-coloured stone, and on every wall, a gilt frame around nothing. Fennick the caretaker shows you the path worn smooth down the middle of the floor. "Nine o'clock to ten, every night, thirty-one years," he says. "She walked it like a prayer." You begin to choose the stops of your own route.

### Week 6: A Face Returns

Halfway down the Gallery tonight, you stop. In a frame that was empty yesterday there is a smudge of colour, like breath on a cold window. By morning it is a woman with a lamp in her hand and a look of fierce patience. The brass plate beneath reads Ysolde. Wren touches the frame and doesn't say anything for a while.

### Week 7: Footsteps Behind

Someone else is walking the Gallery at night. You hear them sometimes, far behind you, keeping exactly your pace, stopping when you stop. When you turn, the corridor is empty. Fennick says it is the old building settling. Fennick does not look as if he believes it either.

### Week 8: The Windows Go Dark

Tonight the high windows of the Gallery fog over one by one, from the outside, until the whole corridor is black. Soft feet at both ends. A calm voice: "Search the frames." You have one way out, and it is the route you have been learning. You will have to walk it backwards, in the dark, without a single mistake.

### Week 9: The Hall of Faces

A round room carved out of the mountain, no windows, three hundred faces cut into the walls by their owners' own hands, and not one name left beneath them. "The Tide can't touch stone," Wren says, holding up the lamp. "But it touched the people who remembered the names. So they might as well be gone." You begin with the first face on the left.

### Week 10: The Scratched Face

Low on the eastern wall, one face has been chiselled into ruin, deliberately and with great care. It is the only one. Wren will not stand near it. She says it gives her a headache, and laughs, and changes the subject, and every time you pass it you can feel her not looking.

### Week 11: A Wall That Walks

Three Salt Guild men in an alley, leaning on a fish-seller. Then a fourth man, enormous and quiet, stepping out of a doorway as if the doorway had been holding him back. It takes about four seconds. "Road-warden," he says afterwards, offering no other explanation, and looks for a long time at your lantern.

### Week 12: Soup on the Quay

There is a long line of hungry people on the Quay tonight, and at the head of it a tall man in a grey hood is ladling soup with his own hands, smiling at each of them as if they were family. Hask has gone quiet beside you. "That one," he says. "That's the one they all follow."

### Week 13: The Kindest Eyes

He knows your name. You never told it to him. He takes your hand in both of his and tells you, very gently, that you are allowed to put down whatever you are carrying. His hands smell of rosemary. When he lets go, you find you are shaking, and you could not say whether it is fear or the strangest kind of longing.

### Week 14: The Counting House

Tall, black-timbered, smelling of old paper and candle-smoke: the Counting House, where every coin in Veyra was written down for six hundred years. Its ledgers did not go blank in the Tide, because nobody can read them. They are written in numbers that are not numbers. Wren opens the first and groans. "Oh, it's going to be one of those months."

### Week 15: Sounds for Numbers

You have begun to see it. The numbers in Calder's margins are sounds, and the sounds are words, and the words are pictures. A bear. A car. A rope. Hask reads over your shoulder, lips moving. "Like road-signs," he says. "Once you know the marks, you can't stop seeing them."

### Week 16: The Closed Eye

The same entry, every month, for nine years: a fortune paid by the Salt Guild into an account marked with a closed eye. Hask puts down his tea very carefully. You have seen that eye before, stitched in silver on the cuff of a grey glove that a Hushed man dropped on the Quay.

### Week 17: The Unfinished Sum

In a rooming house by the salt pans, a clerk who once kept these books sits by a cold grate and cannot remember his own name. On his table: an empty vial, and a note signed with a closed eye. Be at peace. Back at the Counting House, one last column of figures in Calder's hand is waiting, and she never finished adding it up.

### Week 18: The Stopped Clocks

A hundred and twelve clocks in the Clockwork Market, every one stopped at nine minutes past eleven. They are not for telling the hour. They are the Wardens' timetable of the river: when the Tide will rise, how high, for nineteen years ahead. Somebody wanted the city blind to its own weather.

### Week 19: Ticking Again

One by one the clocks start again under your hands, and the market wakes around them like a field after rain. But the Mother Clock in the tower is turning its great iron hands toward a single red mark on its face, and every time you look up at it, you feel the back of your neck go cold.

### Week 20: A Crossbow in the Gallery

You never see him. There is just the flat crack of a bow, and something hissing past your ear, and then a second crack from somewhere else, and a body in a grey hood falling into the square. Below you, a woman in green velvet is lowering a little silver crossbow and smiling up at you as if you had both been introduced at a party.

### Week 21: Dinner at Varre House

Black marble, candlelight, card tables, and Isolde Varre beating Hask at Rook three times running. Then she sends the servants away and tells you about a man who lost his wife and daughter to a fever, drank the grey, and slept for the first time in his life. "Grief," she says, dealing, "is the most dangerous thing in this city. More dangerous than the river."

### Week 22: The Tongues Bridge

A single white arch over the gorge, slender as a swan's neck, and every stone carved with words in a language nobody has spoken for five hundred years. The Tide cannot touch carving. The words are all still here, waiting. You will have to learn to read them the way the Wardens did, one sound-picture at a time.

### Week 23: The Rude Ones

A note arrives from Varre House by a footman in livery: Teach me the rude ones. Wren laughs until she has to sit down on the bridge. It is the first time you have heard her really laugh in weeks, and it echoes down the gorge, and a heron lifts off the river below and flaps away, offended.

### Week 24: A New Carving

Halfway across the bridge, on the downstream side, there is one inscription that is not old at all. The stone is still pale where the chisel bit it. The handwriting, even in carved stone, is unmistakable. You read the first line, and then you stop, and you look at Wren, and you do not want to read the second.

### Week 25: Grey Letters

THE ARCHIVIST BETRAYED YOU. Tall grey letters on every wall in Veyra by morning, and beneath them, smaller: The Order forgives her. Will you? People stand reading them in silent knots. When you pass with your lantern, they turn and watch you, and nobody says good morning.

### Week 26: A Stone Thrown

It comes out of the crowd at the foot of the Archive steps and strikes Wren on the temple. Hask has the thrower by the collar in a heartbeat, and then stops, because it is only Mosk the ferryman, weeping, saying he cannot remember his wife's name. Wren gets up with blood in her eye and takes the old man's hands.

### Week 27: Two Chronicles

Two accounts of the night of the great Tide are passing from hand to hand in every tavern in Veyra. They agree on almost everything. Almost. Somewhere in the small differences, in a time, a name, a laugh or a tear, is the truth, and you mean to find it.

### Week 28: Forty-One Marks

Two palaces, side by side, one for each chronicle. Wherever they disagree, you mark the stop. Forty-one marks so far. And a pattern you do not like: every single difference makes Calder look a little worse. Accidents are not usually that tidy.

### Week 29: A Knock in the Rain

A freckled young man in a soaked grey robe on the Archive steps, shaking so hard his teeth click. He has something wrapped against his skin under his robe. "My name's Ennick," he says. "I'm a Brother of the Order. I think I've stopped being one. Please may I come in? I don't think I can stand up much longer."

### Week 30: Find the Courier

The Order's own secret record of that night, in the Grand Hush's hand. Nine agents in the Archive. A search for something called the Heart. A gate opened a hand's width. And one line, underlined twice: The Archivist has put it in a living ledger. Find the courier. Wren looks at you over the page and doesn't say anything at all.

### Week 31: One Thousand and Eleven Steps

The Tidal Stair climbs the whole city from harbour to Archive, and every evening the Tide floods up it like water up a drainpipe. Children race it for a dare. You are going to race it too, every evening this month, with a longer list in your head each time. Wren has views about stairs. She shares them.

### Week 32: Faster

You are getting quicker. Not by rushing: by trusting the first good picture and moving on. Hask times you from the bottom with a pocket watch and grunts, which from him is high praise. On the landing called the Widow's Rest, you notice grey-robed figures watching from the rooftops, and counting.

### Week 33: They Are Counting

Isolde sends word: the Order knows your route up the Stair, your times, your habits. "Change nothing," her note says. "I mean it. Change nothing at all." Wren reads it twice and frowns. "That's either very good advice," she says, "or very bad. With her I honestly can't tell."

### Week 34: The Widow's Rest

The Tide is rising behind you. The Hushed are coming down from above. Hask is fighting three of them on a landing far below and roaring at you to run. And at the eight-hundredth step, waiting on the Widow's Rest with twenty men, is Isolde Varre. You have never been so glad to see anyone in your life.

### Week 35: Mirrors

They leave you alone in a long hall lined with mirrors. You look into the first one, and it is not your face. It is a kitchen you have never stood in, and a woman you have never met calling you in for supper, and it feels, for one terrible second, like home.

### Week 36: Separate Rooms

The mirrors keep coming, warm and sad and believable, and each one tries to slide into the place where a true memory lives. So you build walls. True memories in your own palace, sealed. False ones in another building entirely, behind a door you label in your mind: not mine. Every hour you walk the true route and count the stops.

### Week 37: Brother Ennick Again

A scrape at your cell door in the middle of the third night. Ennick, white as paper, with a key. "Isolde," he whispers, as if that explains everything, and perhaps it does. "There's a room you need to see. We have about nine minutes. Please walk quickly and please don't touch the mirrors."

### Week 38: A File Marked with a Ruined Face

A locked drawer under the Grand Hush's desk. A file with a scratched-out face drawn on its cover. Inside, one sheet of paper, and one name, and the words Heir to the Heart. You hear water in the drains below the floor, and something heavy being dragged, and Wren's voice swearing.

### Week 39: The Drains at Dawn

Wren reads the file in the dark of the drain by the lantern's light, three times, and then sits down in the cold water as if her strings had been cut. Hask crouches beside her and puts one huge hand on her shoulder. Nobody says anything. Somewhere ahead, faint and grey, is the morning.

### Week 40: Over the Ammerhold

Your face is on posters all over the city: LOST AND CONFUSED. BRING TO THE ORDER FOR CARE. So Hask takes you out by the old road, up through dark pines and over high moors where the heather runs grey and purple to the edge of the sky. It is the first time you have left Veyra since the morning you arrived.

### Week 41: Barrowmere

Half-ploughed fields, the furrows stopping in the middle where someone forgot what they were doing. Children who smile and ask where their mothers are and ask again an hour later. Everyone is kind. Everyone is calm. Hask walks through the village with his jaw set like a trap.

### Week 42: Fenwick Cross

A man mending a fence by the road, slowly and badly, whistling. He looks up at Hask with polite interest and asks if he is lost. Hask stands very still in the road. Then he takes off his pack, picks up the other end of the rail, and helps.

### Week 43: The Waystation Register

An old leather book in the road-wardens' waystation, twenty years of travellers' names. You turn the pages idly by lantern-light. Then you stop. A year ago, almost to the day, there is an entry in handwriting you know better than any in the world.

### Week 44: Back Through the Gate

The city has changed while you were gone. The lamps are still burning. People stop you in the street to ask for help remembering things: a name, a promise, a child's birthday. And on the steps of the great Amphitheatre, with his hood down, the Grand Hush is speaking to a crowd of thousands.

### Week 45: The Challenge

He calls the Rite of Echoes against the Archive. The loser drinks the grey before the whole city. With Calder gone, the keeper of the Archive is Wren. She goes white and steps forward to accept. You step in front of her. "Absolutely not," she hisses. "You absolutely may not." But you already have.

### Week 46: Training for the Rite

Words, numbers, faces, tongues and histories, all in one day, before ten thousand people. Isolde has hired the best coffee-maker in the harbour to keep you awake, and has quietly placed a very large bet. "No pressure, darling," she says. "Only my entire fortune and the fate of the city."

### Week 47: The Day of Echoes

The stone tiers of the Amphitheatre are full from top to bottom. The sun is up. The Grand Hush bows to you from across the sand, courteously, and you bow back. In the front row, Wren is already mouthing the first stop of your route. In the back row, very small, Old Tansy has come to sell her tea.

### Week 48: Deepwinter

Three days to the Night of No Moon. The river behind the Lethe Gate is rising, black and enormous, with a sound like a giant breathing in its sleep. The Hushed have taken the Gate. The Watch will not move against them. Isolde is buying every lamp-oil barrel in the harbour.

### Week 49: The Old Songs

Wren and Tansy sit up all night teaching the Quay folk the old songs of the Long Vigil, the ones nobody has sung in three hundred years. Tansy knows every word of every one of them and cannot tell anyone how. Sevrin's sister, she keeps murmuring. Sevrin's sister knew these. Then she forgets she said it.

### Week 50: Every Route at Once

You realise what you must do on the Night: walk every route you have built this year, all twelve, one after another, without stopping, as a single road. Wren checks you on it, stop by stop, all night long. At the very end of the road, every time, you feel a door that you cannot see.

### Week 51: The Eve of the Vigil

Lamps in every window. Hask oiling the hinges of the Gate stair. Ennick and Tomas Hask arriving together over the Ammerhold, Tomas still smiling, still not knowing why he has come. Wren gives you a single notecard and closes your hand over it. "Don't read it," she says. "Not yet. Just keep it."

### Week 52: The Night of No Moon

No moon. No stars. A wall of black water standing higher than the roofs. A hundred grey robes on top of the Gate, and one man with his hands on the great iron wheel. And in every street of Veyra, for the first time in three hundred years, the people of the city coming out of their doors with lamps.

## Side quests

Side quests finish themselves when the Keeper genuinely shows the skill they ask for.

### The Ferryman's Tally

*Given by Mosk the ferryman, Lamplighters' Quay.*

Mosk has forgotten who owes him for crossings. "Eight names, maybe more. Can you hold a list without dropping a single one? Just once, to show me it can be done?"

**When it is done:** You recite the list back to Mosk without a single gap, and he writes it on the side of his boat in tar, and then, slowly, rubs it out again with his sleeve. "No," he says. "I'll remember it. If you can, I can." He ferries you free for a year.

### Tansy's Remembering Tea

*Given by Old Tansy, Lamplighters' Quay.*

"Here's my recipe," says Tansy. "Don't write it down. Come back tomorrow and tell it to me. If you can, I'll teach you the old song."

**When it is done:** You tell her every herb and every pinch the next evening. She nods as if she expected nothing less, pours two cups, and sings you the Lamplighter's Song in a thin, true voice, and for a moment, under the lamp, she looks forty years younger and terribly sad.

### Your Own Four Walls

*Given by Fennick the caretaker, The Long Gallery.*

"Every Warden built their own route first," Fennick tells you. "Somewhere they knew with their eyes shut. Calder's was her mother's house on the Quay. Have you built yours yet?"

**When it is done:** You walk Fennick through your route aloud, stop by stop, and the old man listens with his eyes closed. "That'll hold," he says. "That'll hold for life, that will." He gives you the spare key to the Gallery's side door.

### The Backward Walk

*Given by Wren, The Long Gallery.*

"Do it backwards," Wren says. "Calder used to make me. She said if you can only walk a route forwards, it's a story, not a place."

**When it is done:** You walk it backward without a single slip. Wren claps, once, and then looks startled at herself. "She said that to me," she says slowly. "Didn't she? When did she say that to me?" She frowns for a long time.

### A Name for the Nameless

*Given by A woman in the Hall, The Hall of Faces.*

A grey-haired woman comes every day to stand before a face in the Hall. "That's my grandfather," she says. "I think. I can't remember his name. Could you learn eight of these, all at once, and give them back?"

**When it is done:** You name all eight, and the fifth is her grandfather, Aldo Brennick, harbour pilot. She cries, and then laughs at herself for crying, and brings you a cake every week for a month.

### The Drifter's Brother

*Given by Joss Hask, The Hall of Faces.*

Hask asks you to learn the faces of the Salt Guild men he is hunting. "I'll need you to know them in a week," he says. "Not tomorrow. A week. That's when it counts."

**When it is done:** A week later, in the market, you see one of the faces and touch Hask's arm. He nods once. That evening he tells you about his brother, Tomas, more words in a row than he has spoken all month.

### The Smuggler's Numbers

*Given by Isolde Varre (by letter), The Counting House.*

An unsigned note: The Guild's couriers change their codes at speed. Can you read ten numbers as fast as they do? Prove it and I will tell you where their wagons cross.

**When it is done:** A second note arrives, scented with something expensive: Impressive. Tuesday, the Fenwick road, midnight. Bring the large one. Hask reads it, grunts, and goes to sharpen something.

### The Salt Guild's Second Books

*Given by Wren, The Counting House.*

Wren finds a second set of Counting House books hidden under a floorboard, in a harder code. "Calder couldn't have read these fast," she says. "You'll need to be better at numbers than she was."

**When it is done:** The second books name every Watch officer the Guild has paid. Wren copies the list into her head, not on paper, and looks quietly pleased with herself for a whole day.

### The Stopped Clock

*Given by Old Pellam, clockmaker, The Clockwork Market.*

The oldest clock in the market will not restart. "It wants its whole number," says the clockmaker. "Sixteen digits, fed in order. No mistakes. It's fussy."

**When it is done:** The old clock coughs, whirs, and strikes thirteen. Pellam weeps a little. "My grandfather built that," he says. "I'd forgotten. I'd forgotten he was a clockmaker too."

### Isolde's Invitation

*Given by Isolde Varre, The Clockwork Market.*

"I only play cards with people who turn up," Isolde says. "Reliably. Show me you can keep a habit, and you're welcome at my table any night."

**When it is done:** You become a regular at Varre House. Isolde teaches you Rook, and how to read a room, and how to lose a hand on purpose when it suits you. You suspect she is teaching you something else as well, and that you will find out what later.

### The Bridge-Keeper's Riddle

*Given by A carving on the bridge, The Tongues Bridge.*

One stone on the bridge bears a riddle in the old tongue: What you learn today you own tomorrow; what you keep a week you keep for life. Learn words that last a week, and the stone will answer.

**When it is done:** You read the riddle aloud in the old tongue a week later, every word still yours, and a loose stone slides out of the parapet. Behind it, wrapped in lead, is a Warden's seal ring, green with age. Wren puts it on her thumb and refuses to take it off.

### Words for Grief

*Given by Mosk the ferryman, The Tongues Bridge.*

After the stone, Mosk comes to apologise. "My wife had a word for when you miss someone," he says. "In the old tongue. I can't remember it. Could you learn enough of the old words to find it for me?"

**When it is done:** The word is "hennoweth": the ache of a lamp left burning for someone who is not coming home. Mosk says it over and over, and then he remembers his wife's name. It was Hennet. He laughs out loud on the Quay, and does not stop for a long time.

### The Forger's Hand

*Given by Brother Ennick, The Scriptorium.*

"The forger always gets small facts wrong," Ennick says. "Capitals. Dates. Little things nobody checks. If you can hold ten facts perfectly, you'll catch every one of his mistakes."

**When it is done:** You catch the forger's seventh mistake and Ennick goes very pale. "That's Brother Hollin's hand," he whispers. "The Grand Hush's own secretary." The forgery and its maker are posted on the Archive door the next morning.

### Brother Ennick's Doubt

*Given by Brother Ennick, The Scriptorium.*

"How do you know when you're wrong?" Ennick asks one night, miserably. "In the Order we were taught never to look back. I don't know how." Show him.

**When it is done:** You show him how you look at your own misses each day without flinching. He starts doing it too, in a little notebook, and then, after a week, without the notebook. "It doesn't hurt as much as forgetting did," he says, surprised.

### Running the Stair

*Given by The children of the Stair, The Tidal Stair.*

The harbour children race the Tide up the Stair every evening. Their champion, a girl called Bree, challenges you: "Fast and right. Both. Or it doesn't count."

**When it is done:** You beat Bree by two steps and she demands a rematch every evening for the rest of the month. She never wins again. She never stops trying. You like her enormously.

### The Masquerade at Varre House

*Given by Isolde Varre, The Tidal Stair.*

Isolde holds a masked ball for the Guild masters. "Three hundred guests, all masked. I need someone who can hold a twenty-room house in their head and know who stood where, all night."

**When it is done:** By midnight you know which Guild master slipped away to which room, and with whom, and for how long. Isolde reads your report with deep satisfaction. "Darling," she says. "I may have to keep you."

### The Second Mirror

*Given by A voice in the Mirror Wards, The Mirror Wards.*

One mirror shows two lists at once, overlapping like ripples. A whisper: Keep the first. Forget the second. If you can, I will let you pass.

**When it is done:** You recite the first list cleanly through the noise of the second, and the mirror cracks from corner to corner with a sound like ice on a pond. Behind it is a narrow passage that leads down to the drains.

### Wren's Lost Face

*Given by Wren, The Mirror Wards.*

"Help me put my face back," Wren says. "In the Hall. I want to carve it myself. But I want to remember it properly first. I want it to last."

**When it is done:** Wren carves her own face back into the eastern wall of the Hall, slowly, over three nights, and under it, her name. When she has finished she stands back and looks at it for a long time. "Hello," she says to it, a little shyly. "It's been a while."

### The Hollow Village

*Given by The children of Stillwater, The Open Roads.*

The children of Stillwater cannot read and cannot remember being taught. Show them, and yourself, how far a mind can come in a single year.

**When it is done:** You teach the children of Stillwater to set a word in a place, a dozen of them in the village square, and the next morning three of them still remember. It is a small thing. Hask watches from the well with an expression you have never seen on him before.

### Hask's Road Home

*Given by Joss Hask, The Open Roads.*

"Things you learned a month ago," Hask says. "Do you still have them? On the road you find out what you really know, because you don't have time to look it up."

**When it is done:** You walk the road back over the Ammerhold reciting a month-old list into the wind, and Hask checks you on every item. At the top of the pass he stops and says, "You'll do," which you later realise is the highest compliment the road-wardens have.

### The Champion's Pace

*Given by Isolde Varre, The Amphitheatre of Echoes.*

"I have placed," Isolde says, "a frankly obscene amount of money on you. Get three of your skills to level five before the Rite and I will feel considerably better about it."

**When it is done:** Isolde doubles her bet. Then she triples it. Then she sends you a coat, black wool lined with green silk, with a note: For the Rite. Lose in this and I will have it back.

### Echo of a Song

*Given by Old Tansy, The Amphitheatre of Echoes.*

Tansy is humming a song she cannot finish. "There's a verse for every skill," she says. "I think. Learn five of them properly, and maybe I'll remember the end."

**When it is done:** She sings the last verse at last, under the lamp, all the way through, and then sits very still. "My brother used to sing that," she says. "I had a brother." Then she frowns, and the frown passes, and she pours more tea.

### What Tansy Kept

*Given by Old Tansy, The Lethe Gate.*

"The things that last three months," Tansy says, "are the things you'll keep for good. Show me something you've kept that long."

**When it is done:** She listens to you recite something you learned in the autumn, and nods slowly. "That's yours now," she says. "Nobody can take that. Not the river, not the grey, not anybody." She pats your hand. "Remember that I said so."

### The Keeper's Year

*Given by Wren, Archivist of Veyra, The Lethe Gate.*

"Three hundred days," Wren says. "That's what the old Wardens had to do to take the oath. Three hundred days of walking the routes. Nobody's done it in three centuries."

**When it is done:** Wren swears you in as a Keeper of Veyra under the copper dome, with the Lamp of Ysolde burning above you both. Afterwards she gives you the notecard from her breast pocket. It has your name on it, and underneath, in her handwriting: In case I ever need reminding. I won't.

### The Keepers' Circle

*Given by Wren, Archivist of Veyra, The Lethe Gate.*

"The Tide leaves a few Forgettings every night," Wren says. "The Circle goes out to meet them. Each of us has helped by remembering. Will you hold twenty old memories for them?"

**When it is done:** Wren puts a small brass lamp in your hands, its glass warm against your palm. "The Circle will always have a place for you," she says. Along the Quay Tansy pours the tea, Fennick jingles his keys, and the lamps burn on.

## A Forgetting on the Quay

The Tide was thin that evening, a few silver threads curling around the lamp-posts of Lamplighters' Quay. Under the fourth lamp sat a small grey shape, round and soft at the edges, like a heap of lint swept up by the wind. It was holding something carefully in front of itself.

"Do not stare," Wren whispered. "It is only shy." She explained that this was a Forgetting, what the Tide leaves behind when it loosens a memory. It does not bite. It simply waits to be remembered.

The thing it held was a picture you had learned some weeks ago, a little blurred. You found you could still say what it was. You said it aloud. The grey shape gave a sigh like a kettle going off the boil, grew lighter, and drifted home along the water. Wren laughed. "See? Not a monster. Just a lost thing."
